The expression "a bridge too far" originated with British General Frederick "Boy" Browning, who said it before Operation Market Garden began in September 1944 [d8]. According to d2 (Wiktionary, citing General Roy Urquhart's 1958 memoir Arnhem), Urquhart ascribed the phrase to Browning, who reportedly admitted to Urquhart: "I think we might be going a bridge too far" [d8]. The phrase was then recorded by author Cornelius Ryan in 1973 while researching his 1974 book about Operation Market Garden, after which it became widely known as the book's title and later a 1977 film [d8][d1][d10]. The expression refers to the Allied attempt to capture a bridge at Arnhem in the Netherlands that proved beyond their reach, and it has since become an idiom meaning an overly ambitious act that leads to failure [d1][d6][d7]. One source (d5) incorrectly attributes the phrase to Field Marshal Montgomery as a retrospective comment, and another (d4) misleadingly claims Ryan "coined" it — but more credible and detailed sources make clear that Browning originated the phrase before the battle and Ryan merely recorded and popularized it [d2][d8].
